title: Maharashtra Completes ₹1,601 Crore Acquisition of Iconic Air India Building in Mumbai
excerpt: The 23-storey Nariman Point landmark, once the airline's headquarters, will be converted into a consolidated government office complex to house scattered state departments.
body:
• Maharashtra government has formally acquired Air India's iconic 23-storey building at Nariman Point, Mumbai, for ₹1,601 crore (approximately $168.5 million).
  • The deal completes a years-long process following Air India's privatisation and transfer to the Tata Group, with proceeds going toward settling legacy airline debt.
  • The state plans to consolidate scattered government offices into the 46,470-square-metre structure, expecting to save nearly ₹200 crore annually in private office rents.

The Maharashtra government has finalised its acquisition of the Air India building at Nariman Point in south Mumbai for ₹1,601 crore, completing one of India's most significant government real estate transactions in recent years. The transfer agreement was signed between Air India Assets Holding Limited (AIAHL) and the state's Public Works Department (PWD) in the presence of Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis at the state secretariat Mantralaya, according to The Hindu BusinessLine.

A Half-Century Landmark Changes Hands

The Air India building, a 23-storey sea-facing commercial tower designed by New York-based architect John Burgee of the firm Johnson/Burgee, was completed in 1974 on reclaimed land owned by the Maharashtra government. For decades, it served as the headquarters of India's national carrier before Air India relocated its head office to Delhi in 2013.

After Air India's privatisation and its acquisition by the Tata Group in January 2022 through an ₹18,000 crore bid, the airline's non-core assets — including this building — were placed under AIAHL, a special purpose vehicle established in 2019 under the Ministry of Civil Aviation to manage legacy debt and properties. Assets valued at ₹14,718 crore, including land and buildings, were transferred to AIAHL to help settle liabilities.

Air India had first listed the building for sale in 2018, seeking around ₹2,000 crore. Other bidders included the Jawaharlal Nehru Port Authority and the Life Insurance Corporation of India, which quoted ₹1,375 crore and ₹1,200 crore respectively. The process stalled before Maharashtra revised its offer upward.

Ending Mumbai's Government Office Crunch

The acquisition addresses a long-standing space shortage for the Maharashtra state government. After a major fire at Mantralaya in 2012, several departments were relocated to rented offices across the city, driving up costs. The state has been in talks to acquire the building since at least 2021.

The cabinet approved the ₹1,601 crore purchase in November 2023, also agreeing to waive approximately ₹298 crore in unrealised income and interest dues owed by AIAHL. The central government granted final approval for the transfer in March 2024. In April 2026, the Finance Department transferred ₹1,600 crore to the PWD to close the deal.

The building's roughly 46,470 square metres of office space will allow the state to relocate departments currently operating from private rentals. Officials estimate annual savings of nearly ₹200 crore in rent.

"The transfer of the Air India building to the Maharashtra government is an important milestone in strengthening the state's administrative infrastructure. The building will be developed as a model government complex with priority given to quality, sustainability and citizen convenience."

— Shivendrasinh Bhosale, PWD Minister, Maharashtra

Structural Audit and Heritage Redesign Planned

PWD Minister Bhosale directed officials to conduct a comprehensive structural audit and complete all necessary repairs before relocating offices. Interior renovation and development work will begin only after structural safety concerns are addressed, he said. He also called for the building's main entrance to be redesigned to reflect Maharashtra's heritage, with leading architects and expert agencies involved in the project.

Currently, nine of the building's floors are vacant. Others are occupied by central government departments — GST and Income Tax offices — which are expected to vacate to make room for state ministerial offices and departments now scattered across south Mumbai.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For generations of Indians abroad, the Air India building at Nariman Point is a deeply familiar silhouette — a symbol of the national carrier that connected India to the world. Its transformation from an aviation headquarters into a state government complex marks the end of an era that began when Air India was a government-owned airline synonymous with Indian global travel.

"This is not only one of the most significant government real estate acquisitions in recent years but also a key milestone in the broader divestment of Air India's non-core assets."

— Kumar Shashwat Singh Sawno, Partner, S&A Law Offices (counsel to AIAHL)

What's Next

Officials said administrative approvals for the renovation are being fast-tracked. The building could be operational within six months to a year after structural work on air conditioning, elevators, and electrical systems is completed. The proceeds from the sale will be used by AIAHL to repay legacy Air India debt, continuing the broader process of unwinding the national carrier's pre-privatisation liabilities.
nri_angle: The Air India building is an iconic symbol for the Indian diaspora — the national carrier's former headquarters that connected India to the world is now transitioning to a new chapter as a state government complex.
